User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: I can walk you through what’s deductible, whether to itemize, how to handle the home office, and which IRS forms you’ll most likely need. I’ll also flag clarifying questions where your answers change the results.

Quick summary (bottom line)
- For federal income tax filing for 2024 you will almost certainly take the standard deduction (it will be larger than the itemized deductions you listed).
- Your photography income is self‑employment income and sho

uld be reported on Schedule C. That allows business expense deductions (including a home‑office deduction), and you’ll owe self‑employment tax (Schedule SE). Those business deductions reduce your net self‑employment income whether or not you itemize.
- Charitable gifts and student loan interest are handled differently: charitable gifts are itemized deductions (only helpful if you itemize), while student‑loan interest (if paid in the tax year) is an above‑the‑line deduction (may be limited by income).
- You’

ll likely need: Form 1040, Schedule C, Schedule SE, (Form 8829 if you use actual home‑office expenses), and the usual information returns (W‑2, 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, 1099‑NEC if issued). See detailed notes below.

Details and calculations

1) Total income (what you reported)
- W‑2 wages: $68,200
- Photography (self‑employment) gross: $16,300
- Interest (Capital One 360): $2,100
- Merrill Edge: $420
Total gross income = $87,020

2) Treatment of the photography income (self‑employment)
- Report on Schedule C (P

rofit or Loss from Business).
- On Schedule C you deduct allowable business expenses (advertising, supplies, business use of vehicle, phone portion, home‑office allocation if applicable, and the $1,050 you listed if those expenses are business-related).
- Net profit from Schedule C is subject to income tax and self‑employment tax.

Estimated example using the numbers you gave (illustrative)
- Photography gross: $16,300
- Home‑office allocation (actual method) of rent: see home‑office section below
- Busines

s expenses (you listed $1,050) — assume business related
Example (using actual home‑office rent allocation computed below):
Net self‑employment income roughly ≈ $11,845 (this was 16,300 − $3,405 home‑office rent portion − $1,050 other business expenses). This is an example only — include any other business expenses you have.

Self‑employment tax
- SE tax applies to net earnings from self‑employment. Rough estimate on the example net income above: SE tax ≈ $1,675 and you may deduct half of that (~$838) as an

adjustment to income on Form 1040.

Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- You may be eligible for up to a 20% deduction of qualified business income (Section 199A) depending on your taxable income and the nature of the business. Photography often qualifies, but the exact amount depends on your final taxable income and other rules. This is more complex — we can estimate if you want.

3) Home‑office deduction (you said 120 sq ft exclusive; home is 740 sq ft; rent $1,750/month)
- You may choose either t

he simplified method or the actual expense method.
  - Simplified: $5.00 per sq ft × 120 sq ft = $600.
  - Actual method: prorate actual home expenses by business use percentage. Business use % = 120 / 740 = 16.216% (about 16.22%).
    - Annual rent = $1,750 × 12 = $21,000.
    - Allocated rent for office = $21,000 × 0.16216 ≈ $3,405. (You can also include a proportional share of utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc., if you use actual method.)
- Since your rent allocation alone (≈ $3,405) >> simplif

ied amount ($600), the actual method will give a larger deduction — assuming you have no reason to use the simplified method.
- To use the home‑office deduction you must meet the rules: the space must be used regularly and exclusively for business and must be your principal place of business (or used to meet clients, etc.).
- If you use the actual method you generally complete Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and attach it to Schedule C. The simplified method does not use Form 8829 but is

reported on Schedule C.

Important: home‑office deductions apply only to self‑employment (Schedule C) or qualifying unreimbursed employee situations (rare since TCJA removed miscellaneous itemized deductions for most employees). Because your photography is self‑employment, you can take this.

4) Charitable donations ($1,500 to Salvation Army)
- Cash donation of $1,500 is deductible only if you itemize on Schedule A.
- For 2024 standard deduction for a single filer will likely be in the ~$14k+ range (check t

he exact 2024 IRS figure), so with only $1,500 of charitable gifts and no mortgage interest or large medical/state taxes, itemizing will almost certainly be LESS advantageous than taking the standard deduction.
- Keep your receipt; for cash gifts of $250 or more you need written acknowledgement from the charity.

5) Student loan interest ($5,100; note: you said 2018–2021)
- Only interest paid in the tax year (payments made in 2024 for the 2024 return) is potentially deductible — up to $2,500 (above-the-line

e deduction may be reduced or eliminated.

6) Unreimbursed expenses ($1,050)
- If these are business expenses for the photography (supplies, gear, travel, etc.) they belong on Schedule C and are deductible regardless of whether you itemize.
- If these are unreimbursed employee expenses (expenses for your W‑2 job), those generally are not deductible for tax years 2018–2025 due to TCJA suspension of miscellaneous itemized deductions.

7) Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Retur

n)
- Schedule 1 (for some adjustments to income, although many adjustments come from other schedules)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — for the photography business
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax) — to calculate SE tax and the deductible half
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual method for the home office
- Form 1098‑E — student loan interest statement (if you have interest paid in 2024)
- Form(s) 1099‑NEC (or 1099‑MISC) — if any clients sent you these

for photography income (you must report the income even if you did not receive 1099s)
- Form(s) W‑2, 1099‑INT (Capital One 360), 1099‑DIV (Merrill Edge), etc. Keep these for your records.

8) Estimated taxes / withholding
- Because you have self‑employment income you may owe self‑employment tax and additional income tax beyond what was withheld from your W‑2. If you expect a tax balance due this year you should consider making quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES) to avoid penalties.

9) Records

to gather
- W‑2 from Coastal Manufacturing
- 1099‑NEC/other records showing photography income (or a totals worksheet if you didn’t receive 1099s)
- 1099‑INT and 1099‑DIV statements
- Rent records and bills, utilities, and any receipts to support home‑office actual expense allocation
- Receipts for the $1,050 business expenses and $1,500 charity receipt
- 1098‑E for student loan interest (if applicable)
- Any other receipts for business expenses (equipment, advertising, supplies)

Questions I need to finali

ze exact answers
1. Were the $5,100 in student loan interest payments made during 2018–2021 (i.e., not in 2024)? If so, none of that is deductible on your 2024 return. If you actually paid interest during 2024, how much was paid in 2024?
2. Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for your photography (i.e., ordinary and necessary business costs), or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from your W‑2 job?
3. Do you have any other ordinary/necessary business expenses for photography (equip

ment purchases, advertising, travel, auto/mileage, software subscriptions, phone, insurance)?
4. Did any photography clients issue you 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC?

If you want, I can:
- Run the detailed numbers (estimate AGI, taxable income, self‑employment tax, and federal income tax) if you answer the questions above and confirm whether you want the actual home‑office method or simplified method.
- Prepare a checklist / draft email to a tax preparer with all the figures and documents.
- Estimate quarterly esti

mated payments for 2025 based on the 2024 projection.

Would you like me to:
A) Estimate your 2024 tax (AGI, SE tax, likely federal income tax) using the actual home‑office deduction and assuming the $1,050 are business expenses and that none of the $5,100 student‑loan interest is deductible? 
B) Or first confirm the points I asked about (student loan timing, expense nature, other business costs)?
